ENGINEERING NOTE · INCREMENTAL SQL

Late data is why incremental models need a lookback.

Loading only dates newer than the latest one in the warehouse is fast. It also means an order that shows up today with yesterday’s business date never gets loaded. So this model re-reads a short window of recent days on every run.

System
dbt Core + DuckDB
Lookback
Three days
Validation
57 tests

01 · THE GAP

Having the latest date doesn’t mean having all the data.

A common incremental pattern reads only source rows dated after the latest date already in the target. That only works if records arrive in business-date order.

Retail feeds don’t always do that. An order can turn up late, after the warehouse has already moved on to a newer date. With a strict high-water mark, that row is never read, and it stays missing for good.

02 · THE WINDOW

Re-read the last three days on every run

On incremental runs, the model reads source orders dated within three days of the latest date in the target. New dates still come through, and orders that arrived a bit late get picked up.

{% if is_incremental() %}
where ordered_date >= (
  select max(ordered_date) - interval '3 days'
  from {{ this }}
)
{% endif %}

The window is a setting you can change. It should match how late data really arrives: wide enough to catch the usual delays, but small enough that the model isn’t rebuilding all of history.

03 · AVOIDING DUPLICATES

Re-reading rows mustn’t create duplicates

If the model just appended, re-reading recent orders would duplicate them. Instead it uses order_id as the unique key with dbt’s delete-and-insert incremental strategy.

Each order in the window replaces its existing row in the target. Corrections and late orders get in, and each order still has exactly one row.

  • Keep money as integer cents all the way through.
  • Keep cancelled and returned orders rather than dropping them.
  • Use a snapshot for customer attributes that change over time and need history.
  • Reconcile order facts against the staged inputs.

04 · HOW I TESTED IT

CI runs the build twice

One clean build only tests the full-refresh path. CI builds the warehouse twice so the second run actually goes through the incremental logic.

Then the 57 tests check contracts, relationships, accepted values and business reconciliation. So the incremental path gets tested on every CI run.
